record_reviews.summary: Darwin introduces himself through Curtis and asks Poole to answer an enclosed set of questions on colours and stripes in Indian horses, especially the Kattywar breed. The enclosure is missing, so the question set itself cannot be reconstructed from the body.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Poole for acknowledging the October 13 request, clarifies that “native horses” chiefly means Kattywar horses, and adds questions about whether the breed is cob-built and whether dark stripes occur on head or near eye. It is a short follow-up, with the earlier acknowledgement and original enclosure absent.

record_reviews.summary: Poole answers from recollection: he distinguishes dun, mouse-dun and cream colours; describes tiger marks on cheeks, nose, withers and legs; gives their fading with age; and discusses shoulder stripes, inheritance and purity of Kattywar horses. He repeatedly limits certainty to personal recollection and local reports.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Correspondent-authored incoming; copied/damaged status qualified by source metadata

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Poole for the detailed information, identifies the wild ass as probably Equus hemionus, asks whether Kattywar horses are cob-built, seeks permission to quote Poole, and asks further about wild-ass stripes and hybrid stripe cases. The questions show which parts of Poole’s answer he is using, but do not make the missing original enclosure recoverable.

evidence.quote: My last note crossed your communication you have fully anticipated my questions about stripes on face.

record_reviews.summary: Poole answers Darwin’s follow-up. He denies that true Kattywar horses are stumpy, gives their height and conformation, describes wild-ass stripes and colour, and reports herd behaviour and local accounts of capture and taming. He explicitly says his observations are from recollection and permits quotation with that qualification.

record_reviews.summary: Smith identifies Darwin’s red-headed ant as Formica sanguinea and the other as F. rufa, discusses the season and conditions for slave-making forays, and describes the cup-shaped foundations and later hexagonal walls of Polistes/Polybia combs. The surviving letter is damaged and its diagram is not fully transcribed; the wasp discussion is distinct from the ant answers.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s four-question memorandum asks Smith about stray fertile Bombus females, stray workers in non-slave-making ant nests, whether F. sanguinea always makes slaves, and feeding behaviour of F. nigra/cunicularia slaves. Smith’s answers are interlined in the preserved memorandum, with his uncertainty and observational limits retained; this is not a normal later incoming letter.
record_reviews.date_assessment: before 1858-03-09; XML lower bound 1809 is a metadata artifact

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Smith whether F. sanguinea slaves forage outside the nest, contrasts Smith’s reported view with Huber, requests permission to quote Smith, and raises the possibility that Huber’s ant is a different allied species. The final request to thank G. R. Gray concerns a missing note and is not evidence of its contents.

evidence.quote: Would you be so kind as to tell me whether you ever saw, the Slaves in the nests of F. sanguinea, go out in search of food or materials for their nest

record_reviews.summary: Smith answers that repeated observations in May, June and August never showed slave ants entering or leaving, so he regards them as household slaves, while allowing Darwin to quote the imperfect observations. He separately reports Stylops in Andrena and identifies the English F. sanguinea with Huber’s species, though the source is damaged and contains lacunae.
